name: Motionmuse
subcategory: AI motion graphics and animated video generation
tagline: AI tool for turning prompts, scripts, or stills into animated video and motion graphics.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Public details on this one are thin and the site did not reliably resolve while this entry was written, so treat everything here as provisional. If the product is what the name implies, generative motion and animated video, then the thing you would be replacing is a video model plus a GPU farm, and neither of those falls out of a coding agent in one session. You can absolutely build a local motion graphics renderer that takes a JSON brief and spits out animated MP4s with text, logos, and transitions, and for a lot of use cases that is the actual job. What you cannot build is prompt-to-motion from nothing, or the render queue that returns a clip in ninety seconds while you go get coffee. The consolation build below is template-driven, deterministic, and genuinely useful, just not magic.
coreLoopDIY: A local Remotion project that reads a JSON brief and renders animated text, logo, and image-sequence motion graphics to MP4 with ffmpeg.
requirements: A machine that tolerates long renders
Your own fonts, logos, and source images
Optional: an LLM API key if you want auto-generated scene copy
whatYouLose: Prompt-to-video generation: a template renderer animates what you give it, it does not invent motion
Hosted rendering, so a one minute 1080p piece ties up your own laptop
Stock asset and font licensing bundled into the subscription
Whatever stylistic presets and taste the product ships with out of the box
Browser editing and sharing: your version is a config file and a terminal
moatNotes: If it is a thin wrapper over a public video model, the moat collapses to UI taste and render credits, which is a much weaker position than it sounds.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay generative video tools because the alternative is either a motion designer at a day rate or a weekend of learning keyframes. Even a mediocre model that produces an acceptable fifteen second clip in two minutes beats a perfect template system you have to hand-author, because the cost being removed is decision-making, not rendering. The GPU time is real money too, and a subscription hides it behind a flat number. That said, if your actual need is the same lower-third and logo sting across fifty videos, you are paying model prices for a job templates do better and more consistently.
notes: A template renderer is a weekend; a video model is not. The moat is the trained model and the GPU capacity to serve it in under two minutes, not the editor around it.
prompt:
Build a local motion graphics renderer in an empty folder. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: TypeScript, Remotion, React, ffmpeg via Remotion's bundled renderer. Package manager: pnpm.

What it does:
1. Reads a brief.json file at the project root describing a video: width, height, fps, durationInFrames, brandColors, fontFamily, and a scenes array.
2. Each scene has a type from this fixed set: title, lowerThird, kenBurns, bulletReveal, logoSting, outro. Each carries its own text, image paths, and durationInFrames.
3. Renders each scene type as a Remotion composition with spring-based entrances, staggered text, and crossfade transitions between scenes.
4. A CLI command `pnpm render brief.json out/video.mp4` bundles and renders to H.264 MP4, printing progress and total render time.
5. A second command `pnpm preview` opens Remotion Studio so scenes can be scrubbed and tweaked live.

Rules:
- Fonts and images load from ./assets. Fail loudly with a clear message if a referenced file is missing.
- Validate brief.json with zod and print human-readable errors, never a stack trace.
- Ship three example briefs in ./examples: a product teaser, a quote card, and a 3-bullet explainer.
- Audio: accept an optional mp3 path per brief and mux it in. No music library.

Explicitly out of scope: any generative video or diffusion model, any hosted render queue, any login, any analytics. If you add an optional LLM step that drafts scene copy from a one-line idea, put the key in .env, gate it behind a flag, and make the tool fully functional without it.

Finish with a README showing the brief.json schema and one copy-pasteable render command.
